opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and they reinforce each other.

The first is just that a lot of the component technology has been driven down in cost by other industries. Motors, batteries, cameras, compute: these have all ridden on the back of consumer electronics, electric vehicles, drones. When I started in robotics, a research arm might cost you hundreds of thousands of dollars, and a big part of that was that you were buying very specialized, very precise actuators and sensors made in small volumes. Now a lot of those parts are commodity items.

But the second thing, which I think is actually more interesting, is that the role of the hardware is changing because of learning. Traditionally, if you wanted a robot to do something reliably, the robot had to be extremely precise. You'd have a very accurate model of the arm, very stiff joints, very repeatable positioning, because the controller was essentially open-loop on top of that model. All that precision is expensive. If instead you have a learned policy that's looking at the world through cameras and correcting itself continuously, then you can tolerate a lot more slop in the hardware. The intelligence compensates for imperfection. A person doesn't have millimeter-precise joints either; we just use feedback really well.

So once you believe that the brain is going to do the heavy lifting, you can design much cheaper bodies. Some of the arms we've used in our research cost a few thousand dollars, sometimes less, and with good learned controllers they can do surprisingly dexterous things: folding laundry, bussing tables, that kind of thing.

And then there's a third piece, which is scale and demand. As more people believe robots with general-purpose learned controllers are actually going to work, there's more investment and more manufacturing volume, and that brings costs down the usual way. It's a bit of a virtuous cycle: better models make cheaper hardware viable, cheaper hardware means more robots in the world collecting data, and more data makes the models better.

I'd say we're still early on that curve. I don't think hardware is the main bottleneck anymore. The bottleneck is really the intelligence, and getting enough of the right kind of data.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a learned policy uses cameras to observe the world and continuously correct its actions, allowing the robot to tolerate less precise hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things going on, and it's worth separating them because they have different causes.

The first is just the components. A robot arm is basically motors, gearboxes, encoders, and a bit of structural material. Those components got a lot cheaper over the last decade, and a big part of that is actually spillover from other industries. Drones, electric vehicles, consumer electronics, phones. If you need a good brushless motor or a decent IMU or a camera, you're now buying something that's manufactured at enormous scale for some other purpose, and robotics gets to ride on that. Fifteen years ago, if you wanted a research-grade arm, you'd pay something like a hundred thousand dollars, and a lot of that cost was that the parts were basically bespoke. Now you can get a pretty capable arm for a few thousand dollars, and the low-cost ones for a few hundred.

The second thing, and I think this is actually the more interesting one, is that the requirements changed. Classical robotics, the industrial stuff, needed incredibly precise, stiff, repeatable hardware, because the control was open-loop in a sense. You programmed a trajectory, and the robot had to execute it to sub-millimeter accuracy because it wasn't really looking at the world. Once you have learning-based systems that are closed-loop on vision, you don't need that. The robot can see where its hand is relative to the object and correct. So you can tolerate backlash, you can tolerate compliance, you can tolerate a cheaper, sloppier mechanism, because the intelligence is compensating for the imprecision of the hardware. That's a big deal. It means the thing that used to be the expensive part, the precision engineering, is now partly a software problem.

And then the third thing is more of a demand-side story. There's a lot more people building robots now, a lot of startups, a lot of labs, and that creates a market for low-cost platforms, which creates competition, and the whole thing starts to compound. You see this with things like the ALOHA-style setups, where people realized you could do serious research with hardware that's within reach of a well-funded grad student rather than a well-funded factory.

I'd caution a little though. The arm costs came down a lot. Hands, dexterous hands, reliable tactile sensing, those are still expensive and still kind of fragile. And the full humanoid platforms, those are getting cheaper, but there's a reliability question that's separate from the cost question. A cheap robot that breaks every two weeks isn't actually cheap. So I think the hardware trend is real and it's very encouraging, but the part I'm most excited about is less that the hardware got cheap and more that we figured out how to make cheap hardware useful.

r001.rationale: It explains that vision-based closed-loop learning lets a robot see its hand relative to an object and correct, so it can tolerate less precise, cheaper hardware.

astra-6.text:
A lot of it comes from components that were developed for much larger markets. Smartphones drove down the cost of cameras, inertial sensors, and computation. Electric vehicles and drones created demand for batteries, motors, and motor controllers. Robotics can take advantage of those supply chains without having to pay for all that development itself.

There’s also a relationship between the quality of your software and how expensive your hardware needs to be. If you rely on very precise, predictable motion, you need tight manufacturing tolerances, expensive gearboxes, and carefully calibrated sensors. If your controller can learn to compensate for imperfections, you may be able to accomplish the same task with cheaper hardware.

That doesn’t mean software makes mechanical engineering irrelevant. Reliability and durability are still hard. But the cheapest robot that can do something useful depends quite a bit on how good the intelligence controlling it is.

r001.rationale: The response says a controller can compensate for hardware imperfections, but it does not connect that compensation to visual feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from components that were developed for much larger markets. Robots need cameras, inertial sensors, batteries, motors, and computers. If you had to develop all of those specifically for robotics, they would be incredibly expensive. But phones, electric vehicles, and other consumer products have driven down the costs of many of those components.

There’s also a feedback loop where, as robots become cheaper, more people can build them, and you start getting more standardized components and more competition. That brings costs down further.

The caveat is that cheap hardware isn’t necessarily reliable hardware. Building a robot that can operate all day without somebody maintaining it is still difficult. But for research, and increasingly for useful applications, the hardware is becoming much less of a barrier. The harder question is how to make it do what you want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lower component costs, standardization, competition, and reliability, but does not explain that visual feedback can reduce the mechanical precision required of robot hardware.
